[1526] There are a few things that are probably just like invariants.
[1530] You know, you've got to like make something people want. That advice was good or agents want one years ago.
[1534] Yeah. OK. Well, yes, but at least by our understanding of the world today, like at some level people. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You got it.
[1543] So there's some stuff that just hasn't changed.
[1547] And then there's a lot of other things like how much work you can get done with one person or two people or whatever.
[1552] That feels totally different.
[1553] And I don't think there has been enough re-examination of that in this sort of startup conveyor belt of Silicon Valley yet.
[1562] As a person who's running a gigantic company and generally probably wouldn't have time for building stuff and it now seems like you are.
[1569] How does that change how you are able to lead or what you're able to do that you can like make stuff on the side?
[1577] I mean, we are not a gigantic company, first of all. Like there's probably, I don't know, like maybe the big tech companies have like a hundred times more people than we do.
[1584] Something like that. But I am way I really believe in if you lower friction a little bit, people build way more.
[1594] And I have really felt that now with dots and these like, you know, little chunks of time I have or even like a long chunk of time where I can like have this interactive thing and a lot done.
[1606] I feel like I will do something that is not just like a little side project for myself like I used to do with Codex, but like I hope I launch something into the world.
[1615] Like I hope I actually make a cool new thing and like get it over the threshold.
[1619] And like does that go out on like Sam Altman dot com or are you talking about like a real like open AI product?
[1624] I meant like I would try to like build a plug-in extension or something and put it out.
[1629] Yeah, that's...
[1630] Maybe I'll ship a real open AI product.
[1632] Feels like all bets are off now.
[1635] And so, you know, you have to make that decision. Do I...
[1638] You know what? I will do that. I'm inspired now.
[1639] Okay, great.
[1640] What's... Do you have...
[1641] No, I don't know. I don't think about it. Now I want to do something.
[1642] I love it. I love it. But you do have to make a decision of like you could just put a team on that.
[1647] So what do you get to... What does that add that instead of having to put a team on it, you can now be like, oh, I'm going to make a plug-in?
[1654] Well, I think today was an example of this. Like you talked about how the amount of stuff every Dev Day has gone up.
[1659] Like we could not have done all of this stuff without having AI to help us.
[1663] And if this works, like next year we will put the teams on it and I will do something and more people will do something and we'll have like a crazy amount of amazing stuff.
[1674] Or just one really great thing. That'd be fine too. But like hopefully the total amount of like utility we put out into the world goes up.
[1682] Do you do all your prompting on Ultrafast?
[1684] I do.
[1685] That's sick.
[1686] Yeah.
[1687] That's crazy.
[1688] No, I've been thinking about this. I worry that in some ways we kind of get out of touch with people building on our tools and we try it. We've tried to like put all of these constraints on ourselves.
[1700] You know, I'm like very aware that not everybody is going to be able to use Ultrafast all the time for everything.
[1706] But I have such a hard time dragging it back over.
[1708] Given that you're like living in that future that I think, you know, all of us can experience a little taste of it.
[1714] What is what is different about the Ultrafast world in terms of how you can use these tools?
[1720] There was an amazing talk like, I don't know, 15, 20 years ago from Brett Victor about kind of the principles that he thought people like how he did his work.
[1732] And one of the things I'm going to get this a little bit wrong, but it was something like creators should have an immediate connection to what they're creating and how speed and the feedback loop was so important.
[1742] And I did not realize what a difference that makes to my kind of iterative thinking loop to have responses come in so quickly.
[1752] But but in terms of trying to build something, trying to think through a problem, it's like a wild difference.
[1757] I know you've been thinking for a long time about AI as a democratizing force to allow anyone to build stuff.
[1765] And in the sort of ultra fast world or in the Astra is a more expensive model world.
[1770] I know you're also thinking about that means something that you pay more for better intelligence.
[1774] So like like what are you thinking there?
[1777] So historically what we have mostly focused on and I think done a great job of is bringing down the like price of IQ.
[1784] And we have made hugely more capable models that get dramatically dramatically cheaper every few months or every year.
[1792] Now there's this new vector that is clearly going to be very important of speed.
[1796] And we are putting the investments in place like our own chip is going to be an incredible contributor to letting us get very fast inference in the hands of everybody to say nothing of what the models will do to improve research and our inference stack and everything else.
[1811] And I think we now realize that we've got to go invest in the democratization of this like we have for model intelligence.
[1818] So when can I expect to use ultra fast for all my prompts?
[1823] You can pay us for it and do it now.
[1826] I don't think I can afford it.
[1828] I think we can deliver 8x at a great price in the not distant future, but then we'll have 100x faster.
[1837] And like, you know, and they'll also be like, you know, GPT-7 galaxy or whatever.
[1843] And so I think I think the right way to think about this is as far as I can see, there will always be a real frontier in terms of intelligence or speed or whatever else at a higher price.
[1858] But I think you can also bet that we will keep doing what we've done of just a ridiculous like put more as a lot of shame, relentless focus on driving value per dollar up and up and up kind of in this big compound anyway.
[1873] Amazing. Sam, thank you so much.
[1875] Thank you.
[1876] Thank you all for coming. I didn't realize there was gonna be like a live audience.
[1883] That was fun.
